title: SQL, the deeper parts
blurb: Window functions, CTEs, reading a query plan, isolation levels and locking: the SQL that turns 'it's slow' into a diagnosis.

questions.q: The scores are ana 90, ben 90, cy 80 and di 70. What ranks does this return, in that order?
choices: 1, 2, 3, 4: every row gets its own number, with ties broken arbitrarily
1, 1, 2, 3: tied rows share a rank and the next rank follows straight on
1, 1, 3, 4: tied rows share a rank and the next rank skips past the tie
1, 1, 3, 3: tied rows share a rank and every later rank is rounded down
questions.why: `RANK` gives ties the same number and leaves a gap, like a sports table. `DENSE_RANK` gives 1, 1, 2, 3 with no gap, and `ROW_NUMBER` gives 1, 2, 3, 4, breaking the tie arbitrarily unless the ORDER BY is unique. Pick by whether 'the second place' after a tie should exist.
questions.asked: The warm-up window-function question; the follow-up is which one you use for 'top 3 per group' when ties matter.

questions.q: In Postgres, SQL Server or SQLite, the rows are (day 1, 10), (day 2, 20), (day 2, 5), (day 3, 1). What `running` values do the two day-2 rows get?
choices: 30 and then 35, as each row adds only its own amount to the rows before
35 on both, as the default frame includes every peer tied on the same day
25 on both, as tied rows are summed together apart from the earlier days
An error, as ORDER BY inside OVER requires a sort key that is unique
questions.why: With ORDER BY and no frame clause, the default frame is `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, and RANGE includes all peers of the current row, so both day-2 rows see 10 + 20 + 5. Write `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` (and a unique tiebreaker) to get a true row-by-row running total of 30 then 35.
questions.asked: A subtle bug in real reports; knowing ROWS vs RANGE shows you have read the frame rules, not just copied a running-total snippet.

questions.q: `daily` holds signups of 40, 55 and 50 for days 1, 2 and 3. What does `change` contain, in day order?
choices: NULL, 15, -5, since the first row has no previous row to read
0, 15, -5, since LAG treats a missing previous row as zero
15, -5, NULL, since LAG reads the value from the following row
40, 15, -5, since the first row is compared with itself as zero
questions.why: `LAG(x)` reads x from the previous row in the window order and returns NULL when there is none, and anything minus NULL is NULL. Pass a default, `LAG(signups, 1, 0)`, if you want 40 for the first day. `LEAD` is the one that looks at the following row.
questions.asked: Period-over-period change is the everyday use of window functions; the NULL edge shows you have actually run one.

questions.q: What is the key difference between `GROUP BY customer_id` with `SUM(total)` and `SUM(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)`?
choices: GROUP BY gives one row per customer; the window keeps every row and adds the sum
PARTITION BY needs an index on customer_id, while GROUP BY works without one
The window version sums only the rows before the current row within each customer
They return identical results, and PARTITION BY is only the newer syntax for it
questions.why: Aggregation collapses each group to one row; a window function computes over the partition but leaves every input row in the result, so you can show each order next to its customer's total. Without an ORDER BY in the OVER clause the frame is the whole partition, not a running total.
questions.asked: The concept that makes window functions click; interviewers use it to see whether you would otherwise reach for a self-join.

questions.q: Which frame gives a 7-day moving average over the current day and the six before it, assuming one row per day?
choices: ROWS BETWEEN 7 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND 6 FOLLOWING
questions.why: `6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` is seven rows. `7 PRECEDING` averages eight, `UNBOUNDED PRECEDING` is a cumulative average, and `6 FOLLOWING` looks forward. ROWS counts rows, not days, so a missing day silently widens the window; fill gaps with a calendar table, or use a RANGE frame with an interval where the engine supports it (Postgres 11+).
questions.asked: Moving averages are a staple dashboard query; the off-by-one and the missing-day caveat are what interviewers probe.

questions.q: The rows (id, parent_id) are (1, NULL), (2, 1), (3, 1) and (4, 2). Which ids does this Postgres/SQLite query return?
choices: 2 only, since the recursive member runs for just a single level
1, 2 and 4, following the tree up to the root and back
2 and 4: category 2 and everything beneath it in the tree
2, 3 and 4, since every row under the root is included
questions.why: The anchor returns 2; each pass joins children onto the rows found last pass (4), and the recursion stops when a pass adds nothing. The join direction decides whether you walk down (children) or up (ancestors). SQL Server omits the `RECURSIVE` keyword and stops at `MAXRECURSION` (default 100); Postgres loops on cyclic data until you add a depth column or, from 14, a `CYCLE` clause.
questions.asked: Category trees, org charts and threaded comments all need this; interviewers want to see you can read the anchor and recursive parts.

questions.q: In Postgres 12 and later, what happens to a non-recursive, side-effect-free CTE that the query references once?
choices: It is always computed first and stored, so outer filters cannot reach inside
The planner inlines it like a subquery, unless you write `AS MATERIALIZED`
It is cached for the rest of the session, so repeat queries skip the work
It becomes a temporary table with its own statistics, gathered at runtime
questions.why: Before Postgres 12, every CTE was an optimisation fence: computed in full, with outer WHERE clauses unable to push down, which is the folklore behind 'CTEs are slow'. Since 12 a single-reference CTE is inlined; `MATERIALIZED` restores the fence and `NOT MATERIALIZED` forces inlining. SQL Server has always inlined CTEs, which are not cached anywhere.
questions.asked: Separates people who repeat 'CTEs are slow' from those who know when and on which engine it was true.

questions.q: This is meant to list customers who have placed at least one order. Ana has three orders. What goes wrong, and what fixes it?
choices: Nothing: an inner join returns each customer row at most once
Ana appears three times; test the orders with WHERE EXISTS instead
Customers without orders appear with NULLs; filter them with IS NOT NULL
It fails without GROUP BY c.name; add it so each name is aggregated
questions.why: A join produces one row per matching pair, so a customer with three orders appears three times. `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)` is a semi-join: it only asks whether a match exists and returns each customer once. Patching it with DISTINCT works but hides the intent and does extra de-duplication work.
questions.asked: Checks you know joins multiply rows; strong candidates reach for EXISTS rather than DISTINCT.

questions.q: In Postgres 11+ or SQL Server, what does `INCLUDE` buy the query below?
choices: status and total become key columns, so `WHERE status = ?` can seek on them
The table is physically re-sorted by customer_id, then status and total
status and total must now be unique within each customer_id in the table
The index alone answers the query, with no lookup into the table per row
questions.why: INCLUDE stores extra columns in the index leaf pages without making them part of the key, so this query becomes an index-only scan (Postgres) or avoids key lookups (SQL Server). They cannot be used to seek or sort, and they widen the index, so include only what hot queries read. In Postgres, index-only scans also depend on the visibility map being current.
questions.asked: Covering indexes are the most common fix for a hot read query; interviewers check you know included columns are not searchable.

questions.q: In Postgres or SQLite (a filtered index in SQL Server), what does this index enforce?
choices: Every email is unique across all rows, whether soft-deleted or live
Deleted rows can never be inserted with an email that is already in use
One live user per email, while soft-deleted rows may share the address
Emails are unique among live rows, and any NULL email is rejected outright
questions.why: A partial (filtered) index covers only rows matching its WHERE, so uniqueness applies among live users and a person can re-register after deleting their account. It is also smaller than a full index. A query can use it only when its own filter implies `deleted_at IS NULL`, so write that predicate literally.
questions.asked: The standard answer to 'soft delete broke our unique constraint'; it shows you can make the database enforce a rule with conditions.

questions.q: `orders.status` has an index, and 95% of rows are 'active'. Postgres answers `WHERE status = 'active'` with a sequential scan. Why?
choices: Reading most of the table through the index costs more than one full scan
The index must be corrupt, since a usable index is always chosen over a scan
Postgres never uses an index for equality tests on text-typed columns
The query is missing an index hint, which Postgres requires to use one
questions.why: The planner costs both options using column statistics: fetching 95% of rows one index entry at a time means random page reads, while a sequential scan reads pages in order once. For the rare 'cancelled' value the same index wins. Postgres has no index hints; a partial index on the rare values is the usual improvement.
questions.asked: 'Why isn't it using my index?' is the most common tuning question; selectivity is the first thing a strong answer checks.

questions.q: After a bulk import, Postgres `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows this slow plan. What is the most likely cause?
questions.code:
Nested Loop  (rows=1) (actual rows=48210 loops=1)
  -> Index Scan using ix_orders_status on orders
       (rows=1) (actual rows=48210 loops=1)
  -> Index Scan using customers_pkey on customers
       (rows=1) (actual rows=1 loops=48210)
choices: Stale statistics: it expected 1 row, so ANALYZE the orders table
The customers primary key index is missing and has to be created
Nested loops are always slow, so disable them for the whole server
The import left orders locked, so each lookup waits on a lock
questions.why: Estimated rows=1 against actual 48,210 is the tell: the planner chose a nested loop for one row and then ran the inner lookup 48,210 times. Autoanalyze has not caught up with the imported rows; run `ANALYZE orders` after big loads. The plan does use the primary key, and lock waits show up as time, not as a row-estimate gap.
questions.asked: Reading estimated vs actual rows is the core skill in plan reading; interviewers hand you a plan to see if you find the gap.

questions.q: In SQL Server, after a restart, a tenant with 10 orders ran this first. Now the tenant with 2 million orders times out on it. Why?
questions.code:
CREATE PROCEDURE GetOrders @TenantId int AS
  SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE TenantId = @TenantId;
choices: Stored procedures cannot use an index on a column compared with a parameter
SQL Server caps each procedure's result set at a fixed number of rows
The small tenant's call is still holding shared locks on the Orders table
The plan compiled for the tiny tenant's value is cached and reused for all
questions.why: This is parameter sniffing: the first call's value shapes the cached plan (say, a seek plus key lookups for 10 rows), which is disastrous for 2 million. Fixes include `OPTION (RECOMPILE)` for that statement, `OPTIMIZE FOR`, splitting the query per tenant size, or SQL Server 2022's parameter-sensitive plan optimisation. Locks would show as waits, not a bad plan.
questions.asked: The classic 'fast in SSMS, slow in the app' mystery; a strong answer names the cause and at least two fixes with their costs.

questions.q: Which anomaly does READ COMMITTED prevent that READ UNCOMMITTED allows?
choices: Phantom reads: new rows appearing when a range query is repeated
Non-repeatable reads: a re-read row showing another's committed change
Dirty reads: seeing changes another transaction has not committed yet
Lost updates: two transactions overwriting each other's changes
questions.why: READ COMMITTED only lets you see committed data, but each statement may see newer commits than the last, so non-repeatable reads and phantoms remain possible. In Postgres, READ UNCOMMITTED behaves as READ COMMITTED, so dirty reads never happen there; SQL Server's `NOLOCK` hint really does allow them.
questions.asked: The entry point to isolation levels; the NOLOCK follow-up is common in SQL Server shops.

questions.q: Within one transaction you run the same query twice. What distinguishes a phantom read from a non-repeatable read?
choices: A phantom is new rows matching the filter; a non-repeatable read is a changed row
A phantom is a row deleted by rollback; a non-repeatable read is one never committed
A phantom happens only in NoSQL stores; a non-repeatable read happens only in SQL
A phantom is a stale cached result; a non-repeatable read is a failed second query
questions.why: A non-repeatable read re-reads the same row and sees a committed update; a phantom repeats a range or filter and sees rows inserted or deleted by another transaction. The SQL standard's REPEATABLE READ may still allow phantoms, though Postgres's snapshot-based REPEATABLE READ prevents them.
questions.asked: Tests precise vocabulary; the Postgres note shows you know engines go beyond the standard's minimums.

questions.q: Under default settings, a long report reads `orders` while another transaction is updating some of its rows. How do Postgres and on-premises SQL Server differ?
choices: Each engine blocks the report until the writer commits, as READ COMMITTED needs
Each engine shows the report the writer's uncommitted rows, to avoid waiting
Postgres blocks the writer until the report ends; SQL Server blocks neither
Postgres reads a snapshot and waits for nothing; SQL Server's reader can block
questions.why: Postgres uses MVCC: readers see the last committed version of each row and never wait for writers. SQL Server's default READ COMMITTED uses shared locks, so a reader waits on a row a writer holds, unless READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT is on (the default in Azure SQL Database), which gives Postgres-like row versioning in tempdb.
questions.asked: Explains many 'the report froze checkout' incidents; mentioning RCSI shows real SQL Server experience.

questions.q: Two transfers like these run at the same moment and occasionally deadlock. What is the standard fix?
choices: Raise both to SERIALIZABLE, so the database queues them one after another
Add an index on accounts.id, so each row lock is taken and released faster
Commit after each UPDATE, so neither transaction holds a lock while waiting
Lock the rows in a consistent order, such as always the lower id first
questions.why: T1 holds row 1 and wants row 2 while T2 holds row 2 and wants row 1: a cycle neither can break. If both always lock the lower id first, the second simply waits for the first to finish. SERIALIZABLE adds more locking (or serialisation failures), and committing between the two updates breaks the transfer's atomicity.
questions.asked: Asks for the mechanism behind deadlocks, not just 'retry'; consistent lock ordering is the answer interviewers want.

questions.q: SQL Server detects a deadlock between two transactions. By default, which one does it choose as the victim?
choices: The one that started most recently, whatever work it has already done
The one holding the most locks, since releasing those frees the most
The one least expensive to roll back, unless DEADLOCK_PRIORITY differs
Neither: both wait until their lock timeout expires, then both fail
questions.why: The lock monitor finds the cycle and kills the transaction with the lowest DEADLOCK_PRIORITY, and among equals the one that has written the least transaction log, so the least work is lost. Postgres works differently: a waiter checks for a cycle after `deadlock_timeout` (1 s by default) and aborts itself. Either way, the victim's work is rolled back and the application must retry it.
questions.asked: Goes past 'retry on deadlock' to how the engine decides, which matters when you set a batch job's priority.

questions.q: Ten workers run this Postgres statement at once to claim jobs. What does `SKIP LOCKED` contribute?
questions.code:
UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running', worker = $1
WHERE id = (
  SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued'
  ORDER BY id LIMIT 1
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
RETURNING id;
choices: Each worker claims a different job instead of queuing behind one row
It skips jobs that failed earlier and were left in a locked state
It runs the subquery without taking any row lock, so it is faster
It lets two workers share a job, and whichever finishes first wins
questions.why: Without it, all ten workers pick the same first queued row and nine block on its lock. With SKIP LOCKED each worker passes over rows another transaction has locked and takes the next free one, so Postgres works as a simple job queue. SQL Server's equivalent is `WITH (UPDLOCK, READPAST, ROWLOCK)`; MySQL 8 also supports SKIP LOCKED.
questions.asked: A practical pattern for job queues without extra infrastructure; interviewers like it because it tests locking in a real design.

questions.q: `stock` holds one row, ('A1', 5). In Postgres or SQLite, what does the final SELECT return?
choices: A1 3 and B2 4, as the conflicting row is overwritten
A1 5 and B2 4, as the conflicting row is left untouched
A1 8 and B2 4, as the new quantity is added to the old
An error for A1, and neither row is inserted as a result
questions.why: `excluded` is the row that failed to insert, so A1 becomes 5 + 3 = 8 and B2, which had no conflict, is inserted as 4. `DO NOTHING` would leave A1 at 5. ON CONFLICT is atomic even under concurrency, and needs a unique index or constraint on the conflict target.
questions.asked: Upserts appear in every sync and import job; reading `excluded` correctly is the basic check.

questions.q: In SQL Server, two sessions run this MERGE for the same new SKU at once, and one fails with a primary key violation. Why?
questions.code:
MERGE Stock AS t
USING (VALUES (@Sku, @Qty)) AS s (Sku, Qty) ON t.Sku = s.Sku
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET Qty = t.Qty + s.Qty
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (Sku, Qty) VALUES (s.Sku, s.Qty);
choices: MERGE runs its INSERT branch before it has looked for any matching row
Neither session sees a match, so each inserts, since nothing locks the gap
Each WHEN branch of a MERGE runs as its own separate, nested transaction
The VALUES source must have its own unique index before MERGE can match
questions.why: MERGE is a single statement but not an atomic upsert: under READ COMMITTED no lock protects the missing key, so both sessions take the NOT MATCHED branch. Add `WITH (HOLDLOCK)` (serializable range locking) on the target, or retry on the duplicate-key error. Postgres `ON CONFLICT` handles this race itself; its MERGE (Postgres 15+) has the same caveat.
questions.asked: MERGE's concurrency trap is a known production bug; knowing HOLDLOCK shows you have been bitten or read the post-mortems.

questions.q: In Postgres, why does this query not use the GIN index on `data`?
questions.code:
CREATE INDEX ix_events_data ON events USING GIN (data);

SELECT * FROM events WHERE data->>'status' = 'failed';
choices: GIN indexes serve only full-text search columns, never jsonb documents
The index covers only nested keys, and status sits at the top level here
Postgres cannot index jsonb columns at all, so every JSON filter must scan
The default jsonb GIN index serves operators like `@>`, not `->>` equality
questions.why: A GIN index with the default `jsonb_ops` supports containment and key-existence operators (`@>`, `?`), so rewrite the filter as `data @> '{"status": "failed"}'`. Alternatively, index the expression: `CREATE INDEX ON events ((data->>'status'))`, a plain B-tree for equality and ranges on that one field.
questions.asked: JSON columns are common now; checks you know an index must match the operator the query actually uses.

questions.q: An import inserts 10,000 rows with one INSERT per row in autocommit mode, and it takes minutes. What is the biggest single improvement?
choices: Add more indexes, so the database finds each new row's slot faster
Wrap the rows in one transaction, or send them as multi-row inserts
Switch the primary key to a UUID, so that concurrent inserts never contend
Run 50 parallel connections, each inserting rows in autocommit
questions.why: Each autocommit waits for a durable log flush, plus a network round trip, so 10,000 commits cost 10,000 flushes. One transaction, a multi-row VALUES list, or a bulk path (`COPY`, `SqlBulkCopy`) removes most of that; in a local SQLite test the gap was about 1,000×. Extra indexes slow inserts, and parallel autocommit still pays per-commit costs.
questions.asked: A very common real performance fix; strong answers mention batch sizes so one giant transaction does not hold locks too long.

questions.q: In Postgres 12+ (SQL Server computed columns and MySQL 8 behave alike), what does declaring `total` this way guarantee that a trigger or application code does not?
choices: `total` is recomputed on every read, so it costs no storage space but can never be indexed
`total` never disagrees with qty and unit_price, and an INSERT or UPDATE that sets it is an error
`total` is filled once at insert time and then kept as a snapshot even when unit_price later changes
`total` acts like a DEFAULT, so an UPDATE that supplies its own value overrides the formula
questions.why: A stored generated column is written by the engine from its expression on every INSERT and UPDATE and cannot be assigned (Postgres: 'cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column'), so no code path lets it drift, unlike a trigger someone disables or an ORM someone forgets. It is on disk and indexable; Postgres 18 adds VIRTUAL (computed on read), which is what SQL Server does unless you say PERSISTED. The expression must be immutable and may not reference other tables.
questions.asked: Derived values that drift from their inputs are a classic data bug; knowing the database can own the formula, and what it refuses to let you do, is the mid-level answer.

questions.q: In Postgres, SQL Server, MySQL 8 and SQLite alike, `discount` is nullable. Which of these inserts succeeds?
choices: Both: CHECK only runs when a WHERE-style comparison is evaluated, and neither insert has one
Only A: 150 is an integer so the type check passes, while NULL fails the BETWEEN range test
Neither: 150 is outside the range and NULL is outside it too, so both rows are rejected
Only B: a CHECK rejects a row only when its test is false, and with NULL it is unknown
questions.why: A CHECK constraint rejects a row only when its condition is false; NULL makes `discount BETWEEN 1 AND 100` unknown, which is not false, so B is accepted on all four engines (MySQL enforces CHECK since 8.0.16). 150 is plainly false and A is rejected. If a missing discount is invalid, add `NOT NULL`; the CHECK alone will never enforce it.
questions.asked: The three-valued-logic trap in constraints; a CHECK that quietly admits NULLs is a common cause of 'how did that row get in'.

questions.q: Postgres `EXPLAIN` shows a Hash Join for a query joining `orders` (2 million rows) to `customers` (50,000 rows) with no WHERE clause. Why is that the right choice over a Nested Loop?
choices: It builds a hash table of the smaller side once and probes it per order row, which beats 2 million index lookups
Hash joins are chosen whenever the tables lack indexes, which means the missing index on customers should be added
Nested Loop only works when one side fits into a single page, so it is unavailable at this table size in Postgres
Hash joins return rows in customer id order, which saves the sort that an ORDER BY would otherwise need afterwards
questions.why: When most rows on both sides are needed, one pass to hash 50,000 customers plus one sequential pass over orders is far cheaper than 2 million random index probes; a Nested Loop wins when the outer side is a handful of rows (a selective WHERE) and the inner lookup is indexed. Hash output is unordered; Merge Join is the one that exploits sorted inputs. SQL Server's Hash Match, Nested Loops and Merge Join are the same trio, and all are chosen by estimated cost, so stale statistics can still pick wrong.
questions.asked: Reading the join node is the second skill after row estimates; strong answers say when each of the three join strategies wins.

questions.q: What does `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at)` assign?
choices: A number from 1 across the whole result, ordered by customer and then date
A number from 1 per distinct created_at, shared by rows with the same date
The count of orders per customer, repeated on every one of that customer's rows
A number from 1 within each customer's orders, restarting for each customer
questions.why: PARTITION BY splits the rows into groups and the numbering restarts at 1 in each, following the ORDER BY inside OVER. It never collapses rows, unlike GROUP BY. Rows tied on created_at get arbitrary distinct numbers unless you add a tiebreaker such as id.
questions.asked: The building block of 'first/latest N per group' queries; interviewers expect you to explain PARTITION BY clearly.

questions.q: Why does this fail in Postgres, SQL Server and SQLite?
questions.code:
SELECT id, customer_id,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                          ORDER BY created_at DESC) AS rn
FROM orders
WHERE rn = 1;
choices: Window functions run after WHERE, so filter on rn in an outer query or CTE
ROW_NUMBER needs an explicit frame clause when it is used with PARTITION BY
The alias rn clashes with a reserved word and must be quoted to be used
PARTITION BY and ORDER BY cannot name different columns in one window
questions.why: Window functions are computed after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, alongside the SELECT list, so neither the alias nor the function is available in WHERE. Wrap the query in a subquery or CTE and filter there. Snowflake, BigQuery and DuckDB offer QUALIFY for this; Postgres, SQL Server, MySQL and SQLite do not.
questions.asked: Everyone hits this once; explaining the evaluation order is what makes the answer more than 'use a subquery'.

questions.q: Salaries in one department are 90, 90, 80 and 70. You want everyone on the second-highest salary. Which function makes `WHERE r = 2` return the 80?
choices: ROW_NUMBER(), because it numbers each row in salary order
DENSE_RANK(), because ranks follow on with no gap after a tie
RANK(), because tied rows share their position in the list
NTILE(2), because it splits the salaries into a top and a bottom half
questions.why: DENSE_RANK gives 1, 1, 2, 3, so rank 2 is the second-highest distinct salary. RANK gives 1, 1, 3, 4, so rank 2 does not exist; ROW_NUMBER gives the second 90 rank 2. Choose based on whether ties should consume positions.
questions.asked: 'Nth highest salary' is a classic; choosing DENSE_RANK deliberately shows you thought about ties.

questions.q: In Postgres, SQL Server or SQLite, `NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY v)` runs over 10 rows. How many rows land in each bucket?
choices: 2, 3, 2 and 3: the extra rows alternate between buckets
2, 2, 3 and 3: the extra rows go to the latest buckets
3, 3, 2 and 2: the extra rows go to the earliest buckets
3, 3, 3 and 1: buckets fill up in order until rows run out
questions.why: NTILE divides the rows as evenly as it can and gives the remainder to the first buckets, one each. It splits by row count, not by value, so tied values can straddle two buckets; for value-based percentiles use PERCENT_RANK or PERCENTILE_CONT.
questions.asked: Quartile reports use NTILE; knowing it buckets by count, not value, avoids a misleading chart.

questions.q: Why does `LAST_VALUE(price) OVER (ORDER BY day)` return the current row's own price instead of the final day's?
choices: LAST_VALUE reads backwards, so the current row is the last one it sees
ORDER BY inside OVER sorts descending unless ASC is written out
LAST_VALUE needs PARTITION BY, and without it the frame is one row
With ORDER BY, the default frame ends at the current row and its peers
questions.why: The default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, so the last value in the frame is the current row (or its last peer). Specify `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`, or use `FIRST_VALUE` with the order reversed. FIRST_VALUE works by default because the frame always starts at the top.
questions.asked: A classic frame trap; explaining the default frame proves you understand windows rather than copy them.

questions.q: `sales` has amounts 10 and 30 for region N and 60 for S. What does `pct` hold?
choices: 10, 30 and 60: each row's share of the grand total of 100
25, 75 and 100: each row's share of its own region's total
NULL on every row, as an empty OVER () has no rows in its frame
An error, as SUM needs a GROUP BY when other columns are selected
questions.why: `OVER ()` makes the window the whole result, so every row sees the grand total without collapsing rows. Add `PARTITION BY region` for the share within a region. The `100.0` avoids integer division, which would truncate shares such as 33.3 to 33 in Postgres, SQL Server and SQLite.
questions.asked: Percentage-of-total is a stock reporting query; the empty OVER () is the neat answer.

questions.q: What does this give each row, in Postgres, SQL Server or SQLite?
questions.code:
SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total,
       SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () AS grand
FROM sales
GROUP BY region;
choices: An error, as aggregate functions cannot be nested inside each other
The region's total, and the sum of every region's total beside it
The region's total twice, as the outer SUM sees one value per group
The region's total, and a running total across regions in order
questions.why: The window function runs after GROUP BY, so its input is the grouped rows and the inner SUM is the per-region total; the outer windowed SUM adds those up across all groups. Plain nested aggregates are an error, but an aggregate inside a window function is allowed. Without ORDER BY in OVER there is no running total.
questions.asked: Mixing GROUP BY and windows is where reporting queries get compact; this tests the evaluation order.

questions.q: `logins` has one row per user per day they logged in. Which idea finds each user's runs of consecutive days (a 'streak')?
choices: Compare each day with LAG(day) and count rows where the gap is exactly one
GROUP BY user and date, and keep groups where COUNT(*) is more than one
Subtract ROW_NUMBER() from the date: consecutive days share one value
Self-join each day to every later day and keep the longest match found
questions.why: In a run of consecutive dates, date and row number both rise by one, so `day - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day)` is constant within the run and changes after a gap; group by it to get each streak's start, end and length. Counting one-day gaps with LAG gives the number of consecutive pairs, not the separate runs.
questions.asked: Gaps-and-islands is the go-to 'advanced SQL' interview puzzle for streaks, sessions and availability.

questions.q: A `products` table has duplicate rows per `sku` from a bad import. In Postgres, which statement deletes all but the newest row per sku?
choices: DELETE ... WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT MAX(sku) FROM products GROUP BY id)
DELETE ... WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY sku ORDER BY id DESC) > 1
DELETE ... WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT MIN(id) FROM products GROUP BY sku)
DELETE ... WHERE id IN (ids whose ROW_NUMBER() per sku, newest first, is > 1)
questions.why: Number the rows within each sku, newest first, in a subquery, then delete the ids ranked 2 or more. Window functions are not allowed directly in WHERE, the first option groups the wrong way round, and keeping MIN(id) keeps the oldest row rather than the newest. Add a unique constraint afterwards so the duplicates cannot come back.
questions.asked: Cleaning duplicates before adding a unique constraint is a real task; interviewers like the ROW_NUMBER approach.

questions.q: The query computes `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC)` but has no ORDER BY of its own. In what order do rows come back?
choices: In an unspecified order; only a final ORDER BY guarantees it
In row-number order, since the numbering is applied to the output
In score order, since the window's ORDER BY also sorts the output
In primary-key order, since window functions preserve storage order
questions.why: ORDER BY inside OVER controls how the window is computed, not the order of the result. Rows often come out in that order because the engine sorted them, but a different plan or a second window with another order changes it. Add `ORDER BY rn` if order matters.
questions.asked: It catches people relying on accidental ordering, a class of bug that appears after a plan change.

questions.q: A paginated API needs the page of rows and the total match count. What does `COUNT(*) OVER ()` add to `SELECT ... LIMIT 20` in Postgres?
choices: The number of rows on this page, at most 20, on every row
The total number of rows matching the WHERE, before the LIMIT
An error, as a window function cannot be combined with a LIMIT clause
The total number of rows in the table, ignoring the WHERE
questions.why: Window functions are computed before LIMIT and OFFSET, so every row carries the full match count and you avoid a second query. The engine still has to find every match, so it is no cheaper than a separate COUNT; on huge results an estimate or 'has more' flag is often better.
questions.asked: Total counts for pagination come up in API design; knowing both the trick and its cost shows judgment.

questions.q: In Postgres, `daily_visits` has gaps (days with no row). Which frame averages the current day and the six calendar days before it?
choices: ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
ROWS BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
GROUPS BETWEEN 7 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, one group per distinct day
questions.why: ROWS counts physical rows, so with missing days it reaches back further than a week. RANGE with an interval offset (Postgres 11+, ordering by a date or timestamp) includes rows whose value lies within six days, however many rows that is. SQL Server does not support RANGE with an offset; fill the gaps with a calendar table first there.
questions.asked: Moving averages over sparse data are a real reporting bug; knowing ROWS vs RANGE by value shows depth.

questions.q: What does `LAG(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at)` return on each customer's first order?
choices: The previous customer's last order date
The earliest order date in the whole table
The order's own created_at, used as a default
NULL, as the partition has no earlier row
questions.why: LAG never looks outside the current partition, so the first row of each customer has nothing before it and gets NULL (or the default, if you pass a third argument). That makes 'days since the previous order' naturally NULL for first orders, which is usually what you want.
questions.asked: Time-between-events queries use LAG with PARTITION BY; this checks you know partitions are sealed.

questions.q: In Postgres or SQL Server, which window on `SUM(total)` gives each order a running total that restarts per customer?
choices: OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at, id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id), with an outer ORDER BY created_at
OVER (ORDER BY customer_id, created_at, id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
SUM(total) with GROUP BY customer_id, created_at ORDER BY created_at
questions.why: PARTITION BY restarts per customer, ORDER BY makes it cumulative, and a ROWS frame with a unique tiebreaker adds one row at a time even when timestamps tie. Without ORDER BY the sum is the customer's grand total on every row; without PARTITION BY it keeps running across customers.
questions.asked: Running totals are the most common window-function task; the tiebreaker is what separates a careful answer.

questions.q: What does the WINDOW clause buy you in this Postgres, MySQL 8 or SQLite query?
questions.code:
SELECT day,
  AVG(v) OVER w AS avg7,
  MAX(v) OVER w AS max7
FROM metrics
WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY day ROWS 6 PRECEDING);
choices: It caches the window results so that later queries reuse them
It names one window definition so that several functions share it
It forces the two functions to run in parallel over the window
It creates a temporary view named w that lasts for the rest of the session
questions.why: A named window avoids repeating the same PARTITION BY, ORDER BY and frame, and makes it obvious the functions use the same one, which also lets the engine sort once. SQL Server added the WINDOW clause in 2022 (compatibility level 160).
questions.asked: A readability question; strong candidates know the clause exists and keep report SQL tidy.

questions.q: In Postgres, what does `percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount)` compute?
choices: The average amount of the lower half of the rows, ordered by amount
The value exactly halfway between the minimum and maximum amount
The median, interpolating between the two middle values when needed
The amount that appears most often among all the rows in the group
questions.why: percentile_cont is an ordered-set aggregate that returns a continuous percentile, so with an even count it averages the two middle values; percentile_disc returns an actual row value instead. SQL Server has PERCENTILE_CONT only as a window function, with OVER (PARTITION BY ...).
questions.asked: Medians are asked when averages mislead (response times, salaries); knowing the syntax per engine is a plus.

questions.q: `o` has orders (id 1, paid, oldest) and (id 2, void, newest) for one customer. The goal is each customer's newest order, if it is paid. What does this return?
choices: Nothing, because the customer's newest order is void
Orders 1 and 2, because the filter and the numbering disagree
Order 2, because numbering happens before the WHERE
Order 1, because WHERE filters before rows are numbered
questions.why: WHERE runs before the window, so the void order is gone and the paid one becomes number 1: the query answers 'newest paid order', not 'newest order, if paid'. For the second meaning, number all orders in the subquery and test `rn = 1 AND status = 'paid'` outside it.
questions.asked: Filtering before or after ranking changes the business meaning; this checks you can tell the two apart.

questions.q: What is the main reason to write a non-recursive CTE (`WITH x AS (...)`) instead of a nested subquery?
choices: Readability: the steps are named and listed top-down, and reusable
It is always faster, because the CTE result is cached for the query
It is the only way to use a subquery's columns in the outer SELECT
It runs in its own transaction, so a failure cannot affect the rest
questions.why: A CTE is mainly a way to name intermediate results so a long query reads as steps, and to reference one result more than once. Whether it is inlined or materialised depends on the engine and version, so it is not automatically faster or slower than a subquery.
questions.asked: A warm-up; the follow-up is usually what the engine does with it, so avoid claiming it is always cached.

questions.q: In SQL Server, a CTE that runs an expensive aggregate is referenced twice in the main query. What happens?
choices: The CTE is computed once and stored in tempdb for both references
The CTE's query is typically expanded and evaluated for each reference
It is an error to reference the same CTE more than once in a single query
SQL Server creates an indexed view for the CTE on the first reference
questions.why: SQL Server treats a CTE like an inline view and does not materialise it, so two references usually mean two evaluations. If that is costly, put the result in a temp table first. Postgres 12+ materialises a CTE by default only when it is referenced more than once, and lets you choose with MATERIALIZED / NOT MATERIALIZED.
questions.asked: Knowing CTEs are not caches in SQL Server explains surprising plans; the temp-table fix is the practical part.

questions.q: A recursive CTE walks a `categories` tree, but bad data contains a cycle (A is B's parent and B is A's). What happens by default?
choices: The engine detects the repeated row and stops walking quietly
The CTE returns each category once, as UNION ALL removes repeats
Postgres runs until stopped; SQL Server errors after 100 levels
Postgres errors at once, and SQL Server returns the partial tree
questions.why: Nothing stops a UNION ALL recursion that keeps finding rows. SQL Server enforces a default MAXRECURSION of 100 and raises an error; Postgres runs until it exhausts memory or a statement timeout. Guard with a depth column, UNION instead of UNION ALL when rows repeat exactly, or Postgres 14's CYCLE clause.
questions.asked: Hierarchies in real data do get cycles; knowing the guards shows you have run recursive queries in production.

questions.q: In Postgres, what is the idiomatic way to produce one row per day for a month, so days with no orders show as zero?
choices: SELECT DISTINCT created_at::date FROM orders, filling gaps in app code
An INNER JOIN from orders to a calendar table, which keeps the empty days
GROUP BY created_at::date WITH ROLLUP, which adds the missing days
A LEFT JOIN from generate_series(start, end, interval '1 day') to orders
questions.why: generate_series builds the full date spine, and a LEFT JOIN plus `COUNT(o.id)` gives zero for empty days. SQL Server 2022 has GENERATE_SERIES for integers, and elsewhere a recursive CTE or a permanent calendar table does the job. Selecting from orders alone can never return a day with no orders.
questions.asked: Charts with missing days are a common bug; a date spine is the standard answer.

questions.q: In SQL Server, how do you write a recursive CTE?
choices: WITH tree AS (anchor UNION ALL recursive part): no RECURSIVE keyword
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (anchor UNION ALL recursive part), as in Postgres
CONNECT BY PRIOR id = parent_id after the anchor SELECT statement
Recursive CTEs are unsupported; hierarchies need a WHILE loop
questions.why: SQL Server infers recursion when the CTE references itself; writing RECURSIVE is a syntax error there, while Postgres, MySQL 8 and SQLite require it. CONNECT BY is Oracle's older syntax. SQL Server also offers the hierarchyid type for trees.
questions.asked: Moving recursive SQL between engines trips on this; it is a quick check of cross-engine experience.

questions.q: In a recursive CTE over `categories (id, parent_id, name)`, how do you also return each node's depth and its breadcrumb path?
choices: Call ROW_NUMBER() in the recursive part, which numbers each level in turn
Add depth and path columns: anchor sets 0 and name; each step adds 1 and appends
Use COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY parent_id) in the final SELECT to get depth
Recursive CTEs can only return the columns of the table they walk
questions.why: A recursive CTE can carry computed columns: the anchor starts them, and the recursive member derives each row's value from its parent's, such as `s.depth + 1` and `s.path || ' > ' || c.name`. Casting the anchor's path to a wide type avoids length errors in SQL Server.
questions.asked: Breadcrumbs and indented trees are real UI needs; carrying state through recursion is the key technique.

questions.q: What does this Postgres statement do?
choices: It errors, as a CTE may contain only a SELECT statement
It copies the old orders to the archive and leaves them in place
It moves the old orders to the archive in one atomic statement
It deletes the old orders, and the INSERT sees an empty CTE
questions.why: Postgres allows data-modifying statements in WITH; RETURNING feeds the deleted rows to the INSERT, and the whole statement is atomic. SQL Server gets the same effect with `DELETE ... OUTPUT deleted.* INTO orders_archive`. For millions of rows, batch it to keep locks and WAL manageable.
questions.asked: Archiving jobs are common; knowing a single atomic statement can move rows is a practical Postgres skill.

questions.q: In Postgres, what does `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (... LIMIT 3) ON true` let you do that a plain subquery join cannot?
questions.code:
SELECT c.name, o.id, o.total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT id, total FROM orders
  WHERE customer_id = c.id
  ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 3
) o ON true;
choices: Run the subquery once for all customers, then join the three results
Keep only customers with exactly three orders, as LIMIT acts as a filter
Return three customers per order, as LATERAL reverses the join direction
Refer to c inside the subquery, so it returns three orders per customer
questions.why: LATERAL lets a subquery in FROM reference earlier tables, so it runs per customer and its LIMIT applies per customer. With an index on (customer_id, created_at) that is very efficient. SQL Server spells it CROSS APPLY / OUTER APPLY; LEFT ... ON true keeps customers with no orders.
questions.asked: Top-N per group has two idioms, window functions and LATERAL; knowing both and when each wins is a strong signal.

questions.q: In SQL Server, what is the difference between CROSS APPLY and OUTER APPLY?
choices: CROSS APPLY drops left rows with no result; OUTER APPLY keeps them
CROSS APPLY runs the function once; OUTER APPLY runs it per row
CROSS APPLY returns the Cartesian product; OUTER APPLY joins on keys
CROSS APPLY is read-only; OUTER APPLY may call modifying functions
questions.why: Both evaluate the right-hand expression per left row and may reference its columns. CROSS APPLY behaves like an inner join, removing rows where it returns nothing; OUTER APPLY behaves like a LEFT JOIN, returning NULLs. They match Postgres's CROSS JOIN LATERAL and LEFT JOIN LATERAL.
questions.asked: APPLY is everywhere in SQL Server code; this checks you know which one silently drops rows.

questions.q: What does Postgres's `DISTINCT ON` do here?
questions.code:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id)
       customer_id, id, created_at
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC;
choices: It returns every order, sorted by customer, with duplicates removed
It returns one row per customer: the first in the ORDER BY, the newest
It returns one row per customer, but which one is left unspecified
It errors, as DISTINCT ON needs every selected column listed inside its ON
questions.why: DISTINCT ON keeps the first row of each group of equal ON values, where 'first' is set by the ORDER BY, whose leading columns must match the ON list. It is Postgres-only; elsewhere use ROW_NUMBER. Without a deciding ORDER BY, the row kept would be arbitrary.
questions.asked: A concise Postgres idiom for 'latest per group'; interviewers on Postgres teams often expect it.

questions.q: In Postgres or SQL Server, what extra rows does `GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, city)` add?
choices: Every combination of region and city, including ones with no rows
One subtotal per city across every region, and nothing else
One subtotal per region (city NULL) and a grand total (both NULL)
A running total for each city, in the order the rows were stored
questions.why: ROLLUP produces the grouping sets (region, city), (region) and (), so you get detail rows, region subtotals and a grand total in one query. CUBE adds every combination, including per-city totals across regions, and GROUPING SETS lets you list exactly which you want. MySQL writes `WITH ROLLUP`.
questions.asked: Subtotals are a staple of reporting; knowing ROLLUP saves you a UNION of three queries.

questions.q: A ROLLUP report has rows where `city` is NULL. How do you tell a subtotal row from a real group whose city is NULL?
choices: Subtotal rows always come last, so their position identifies them
You cannot; replace NULL cities with a placeholder before grouping
Check COUNT(city): it is zero on subtotal rows and positive otherwise
Use GROUPING(city), which is 1 on rows where city was rolled up
questions.why: GROUPING(col) returns 1 when the column is aggregated away in that row and 0 when it is a real grouping value, NULL or not. Use it to label rows ('All cities') without confusing them with missing data. COUNT(city) is also zero for a real NULL-city group, so it cannot tell them apart.
questions.asked: A deeper reporting question; it combines grouping sets with NULL semantics, which strong candidates handle cleanly.

questions.q: How do you produce one row per order with its product names as a comma-separated list, in Postgres and SQL Server 2017+?
choices: STRING_AGG(name, ', ') in both, with the ordering syntax differing
GROUP_CONCAT(name) in both, which is the ANSI standard spelling
CONCAT(name, ', ') with GROUP BY, which joins the grouped values
ARRAY_AGG(name) in both engines, then TRIM to strip off the array brackets
questions.why: Both have STRING_AGG: Postgres orders it with `STRING_AGG(name, ', ' ORDER BY name)`, SQL Server with `WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY name)`. MySQL and SQLite use GROUP_CONCAT. Without an order the list order is arbitrary, which makes snapshot tests flaky.
questions.asked: Everyday reporting need; knowing the ordering syntax and the MySQL name shows breadth.

questions.q: `amount` rows for one region are 10 and 30. What does `SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region)` put on each of them?
choices: 10 and 40, a running total down the partition
40 on each, the partition's total on every row
40 once, collapsed into a single row for the region
10 and 30, since no ORDER BY means no summing
questions.why: Without ORDER BY the frame is the whole partition, so each row carries the region total and no rows are removed. Adding ORDER BY switches to a cumulative frame and gives the running total. Collapsing to one row is what GROUP BY does.
questions.asked: Checks you know ORDER BY inside OVER changes the frame, not just the sort.

questions.q: `LEAD(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY session_id ORDER BY created_at)` is used on a `page_views` table. What is it typically for?
choices: Removing duplicate views that share a session and a timestamp
Finding the first view of each session, to identify the landing page
Finding the time of the next view in the session, to measure time on page
Counting the views in each session, which it then returns on every row
questions.why: LEAD reads the following row in the window, so subtracting created_at from it gives the time until the next view; the last view in a session gets NULL. FIRST_VALUE gives the landing page, and COUNT(*) OVER gives the per-session count.
questions.asked: Event analytics is a common place for window functions; this checks you can map LEAD to a real metric.

questions.q: There is an index on `orders (customer_id, created_at)`. What does it do for this query?
questions.code:
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
choices: It finds customer 42's rows, but a separate sort is still needed for ORDER BY
It helps only the ORDER BY, since the equality filter uses the primary key
Nothing: an index cannot serve a DESC order when it was built ascending
It finds customer 42's rows already in date order, so no sort step is needed
questions.why: Within one customer_id the index entries are sorted by created_at, so the engine can read them backwards and stop after 20, with no sort at all. B-trees can be walked in either direction. Sorting on a column not in the index after the equality (such as total) does need a sort step.
questions.asked: 'Latest N for this user' is the most common query in CRUD apps; designing its index is a core skill.

questions.q: The only index is on `orders (status, created_at)`. In Postgres 17 or SQL Server, why does `WHERE created_at > now() - interval '1 day'` not seek on it?
choices: created_at is not the leading column, so the entries are not sorted by it
Range predicates can never use an index; only equality can
The index was built before the rows it would need were inserted
Composite indexes are only used when every one of their columns is filtered
questions.why: A composite index is sorted by the first column, then the second within it, so recent rows are spread across every status. The planner may scan the whole index but cannot seek. Postgres 18's skip scan can jump through a few distinct leading values; otherwise add an index led by created_at.
questions.asked: Column order in composite indexes is asked constantly; mentioning Postgres 18 skip scan shows you are current.

questions.q: In Postgres, you create `CREATE INDEX ix_users_email_lower ON users (lower(email))`. Which query can use it?
choices: SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1
SELECT * FROM users WHERE lower(email) = lower($1)
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email ILIKE $1
SELECT * FROM users WHERE upper(email) = upper($1)
questions.why: An expression index stores the computed value, so the query must use the same expression for the planner to match it. `email = $1` needs a plain index on email, ILIKE is a different operator, and upper() is a different expression. SQLite supports expression indexes too; in SQL Server index a computed column.
questions.asked: Case-insensitive lookups are everywhere; the expression index is the fix for the non-sargable LOWER() query.

questions.q: In SQL Server, `Email` is `varchar(200)` with an index, and the app sends the parameter as `nvarchar(4000)`. Why is the lookup a scan?
choices: The long parameter length makes the optimiser distrust the index statistics
varchar columns cannot be sought with any parameter at all
nvarchar ranks higher, so the column is converted on every row
Parameters always prevent seeks, so the query should be inlined
questions.why: Data-type precedence converts the varchar column to nvarchar, not the parameter to varchar, and converting the column defeats a normal seek (the plan shows CONVERT_IMPLICIT). Send the parameter with the column's type, for example by setting the parameter DbType or column type in EF Core or Dapper.
questions.asked: Implicit conversion is one of the most common real SQL Server performance problems; spotting it in a plan impresses.

questions.q: In Postgres, why is this slow, and what is the sargable rewrite?
questions.code:
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE created_at::date = '2026-03-14';
choices: Casting in WHERE is invalid; use CONVERT(date, created_at) instead
The date literal needs a time zone suffix before any index can match
Dates must be passed as parameters, because a literal always forces a sequential scan
The cast hides the column from its index; use created_at >= day AND < next day
questions.why: Applying a cast or function to the column means the index on created_at cannot be searched for the result. A half-open range `created_at >= '2026-03-14' AND created_at < '2026-03-15'` uses the index and also handles fractional seconds. An expression index on the cast is the alternative.
questions.asked: Date filtering is where most non-sargable predicates hide; the half-open range is the pattern to know.

questions.q: In SQL Server, which predicate lets an index on `CreatedAt` be used for a seek?
choices: WHERE CreatedAt >= '2026-01-01' AND CreatedAt < '2027-01-01'
WHERE CONVERT(char(4), CreatedAt, 120) = '2026' -- ISO style
WHERE YEAR(CreatedAt) = 2026
WHERE DATEDIFF(year, CreatedAt, '2026-01-01') = 0
questions.why: Only the range leaves the column bare, so the optimiser can seek to the start and read to the end. The function forms have to compute a value for every row. SQL Server does special-case CAST(col AS date), but relying on that is less clear than writing the range.
questions.asked: Sargability is the concept behind half of all 'why is my query slow' answers; this is the entry-level form.

questions.q: Postgres has separate indexes on `email` and on `phone`. How can it answer `WHERE email = $1 OR phone = $2` efficiently?
choices: It cannot use either index, as OR always forces a sequential scan
It combines them in a BitmapOr of two bitmap index scans
It uses only the index on the first column named in the OR
It needs a composite index on (email, phone) to handle the OR
questions.why: Postgres can scan each index into a bitmap, OR the bitmaps, and then visit the matching table pages once. A composite (email, phone) index does not help the phone half, because phone is not leading. In engines that handle OR poorly, rewriting as a UNION of two indexed queries is the classic fix.
questions.asked: OR conditions defeating indexes is a common complaint; knowing bitmap scans and the UNION rewrite shows depth.

questions.q: Postgres shows `Index Only Scan ... Heap Fetches: 98000` for a query the index should fully cover. What is the likely cause?
choices: The index is missing a column, so each row is read from the table
The index is corrupt, and a REINDEX is needed to rebuild all of its entries
The visibility map is stale, so it still checks the table; VACUUM fixes it
Heap fetches are normal for index-only scans and cost almost nothing
questions.why: Postgres indexes do not store visibility, so an index-only scan checks the visibility map and must visit the table page for any page not marked all-visible. After heavy writes, until VACUUM runs, most pages are not marked. Tuning autovacuum on busy tables keeps index-only scans effective.
questions.asked: A deep Postgres question; linking index-only scans to VACUUM shows you understand MVCC's costs.

questions.q: A SQL Server actual plan shows an Index Seek feeding a Key Lookup that runs 50,000 times. What does the Key Lookup mean?
choices: The index covers the query, and the lookup only validates the keys
The seek failed, so SQL Server fell back to scanning the table key by key instead
The foreign keys are being checked row by row against the parent table
For each row found, SQL Server fetches missing columns from the clustered index
questions.why: The nonclustered index found the rows but lacked some selected or filtered columns, so each row needs a trip to the clustered index. At 50,000 rows that is costly; add the missing columns with INCLUDE, or select fewer columns. The optimiser switches to a scan when the lookups would cost more.
questions.asked: Key Lookups are the most common thing to fix in a SQL Server plan; covering indexes are the expected answer.

questions.q: Postgres uses a Seq Scan on a 200-row `countries` table even though `code` is indexed. Should you worry?
choices: No: for a table that fits in a page or two, a scan is the cheapest plan
Yes: a sequential scan means the index is broken and should be rebuilt
Yes: force the index with SET enable_seqscan = off for the application
No: by rule, Postgres never uses an index on a table with fewer than 10,000 rows
questions.why: The planner costs each option, and reading a couple of pages sequentially beats walking an index and then fetching rows. There is no fixed row threshold; it is a cost estimate. Turning off seqscan is a diagnostic tool for a session, never a production setting.
questions.asked: Checks that you don't treat every Seq Scan as a problem, which is a sign of plan-reading maturity.

questions.q: What is the key risk of running `EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM orders WHERE ...` in Postgres?
choices: It locks the table until the plan output is read by the client
It deletes the rows, because ANALYZE runs the statement for real
It updates table statistics, which may change other queries' plans
None: EXPLAIN never executes the statement it is explaining
questions.why: EXPLAIN alone only plans; EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement to measure real timings and row counts. For writes, wrap it in BEGIN ... ROLLBACK. The name is confusing: the ANALYZE command collects statistics, but EXPLAIN's ANALYZE option means 'run it'.
questions.asked: A safety question with teeth; people have deleted production data this way.

questions.q: In `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` output, what does `Buffers: shared hit=120 read=48000` tell you?
choices: 120 rows came from the table and 48,000 from indexes
The query ran 120 times and read 48,000 rows on each
120 pages were in memory and 48,000 were read from outside it
120 dirty pages were written back to disk and 48,000 pages were read
questions.why: Shared hits were found in Postgres's buffer cache; reads had to come from the OS cache or disk. A high read count explains why the first run is slow and later runs are fast. Pages are 8 kB, so 48,000 reads is about 375 MB of I/O, which is often the real cost.
questions.asked: BUFFERS turns 'it's slow sometimes' into a caching explanation; interviewers like candidates who use it.

questions.q: A Postgres plan shows an inner `Index Scan ... (actual time=0.020..0.025 rows=1 loops=40000)`. How much time did that node take in total?
choices: About 0.025 ms, as the actual time covers every loop
It cannot be told from the plan without running it again
About 40 seconds, as each loop costs 1 ms plus the time
About 1 second: roughly 0.025 ms per loop times 40,000
questions.why: For nodes executed repeatedly, the actual time and rows are averages per loop, so multiply by loops for the total. A cheap-looking inner index scan inside a nested loop is often where the time goes. Tools such as explain.depesz.com do this arithmetic for you.
questions.asked: Misreading per-loop timings is the most common plan-reading error; getting it right shows real practice.

questions.q: In Postgres, `city` and `postcode` are strongly correlated, and the planner badly underestimates rows for `WHERE city = $1 AND postcode = $2`. What fixes the estimate?
choices: CREATE STATISTICS on (city, postcode) with dependencies, then ANALYZE
Raising work_mem, so the planner can hold more statistics in memory
A composite index on (city, postcode), which also stores statistics
Running VACUUM FULL, which rebuilds the per-column histograms from scratch
questions.why: By default Postgres assumes columns are independent and multiplies their selectivities, which underestimates correlated filters. Extended statistics (`CREATE STATISTICS s (dependencies) ON city, postcode FROM addresses`) teach it the correlation. An index on an expression gathers statistics on that expression, but a plain composite index does not fix this.
questions.asked: A deep planner question; knowing the independence assumption explains a whole class of bad plans.

questions.q: A Postgres plan shows `Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 850MB`. What does it mean and what is the first thing to try?
choices: The table is too large to sort; add a LIMIT to the query
The sort spilled to disk; add an index for the ORDER BY or raise work_mem
The sort is being done by the operating system; restart Postgres
The disk is almost full, so Postgres had to sort the rows in smaller batches
questions.why: The rows to sort did not fit in work_mem, so Postgres sorted in temporary files. An index that supplies the order avoids the sort entirely; raising work_mem for that session helps otherwise. Raise it globally with care, since each sort or hash in each connection can use that much.
questions.asked: Spilling sorts are a common cause of slow reports; the work_mem caveat shows you understand the memory model.

questions.q: In SQL Server Management Studio, what is the difference between the estimated and the actual execution plan?
choices: The estimated plan uses statistics; the actual plan uses no statistics at all
The estimated plan is from the cache; the actual plan is always freshly compiled
The estimated plan is compiled without running; the actual one adds runtime row counts
They show different operators, because the actual plan is chosen only after execution has ended
questions.why: Both show the same plan shape for the same compilation, but only the actual plan runs the query and records actual rows, executions and warnings such as spills. Comparing estimated with actual rows per operator is the core of diagnosing a bad plan.
questions.asked: A baseline SQL Server tooling question; estimated vs actual rows is the follow-up.

questions.q: A SQL Server stored procedure suffers from parameter sniffing: its plan suits some values badly. Which is a standard targeted fix?
choices: Rebuild every index nightly, so the plan cache is cleared each day
Mark the procedure WITH ENCRYPTION, which disables plan caching for every statement
Replace the parameters with string concatenation of the literal values
Add OPTION (RECOMPILE) to the statement, or OPTIMIZE FOR a typical value
questions.why: RECOMPILE builds a fresh plan per execution for that statement, trading CPU for a plan fitted to each value; OPTIMIZE FOR (or OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN) pins the plan to a chosen value or the average. SQL Server 2022's Parameter Sensitive Plan optimisation can cache several plans automatically. Concatenating values reintroduces injection risk.
questions.asked: A follow-up to 'what is parameter sniffing'; naming the fixes and their costs is what interviewers look for.

questions.q: In Postgres, what is a 'dead tuple', and what removes it?
choices: An old row version left by an UPDATE or DELETE; VACUUM reclaims its space
A row that failed a constraint check; it is removed by the next ROLLBACK
An index entry that points at a dropped column; REINDEX removes it
A row that no query has read for a month; autovacuum moves it out to cold storage
questions.why: Postgres's MVCC writes a new row version on UPDATE and marks the old one dead once no transaction can see it. VACUUM (usually autovacuum) marks the space reusable. Long-running transactions stop VACUUM cleaning up, which is how tables bloat.
questions.asked: Understanding dead tuples explains bloat and why idle-in-transaction connections are harmful.

questions.q: In Postgres, how does plain `VACUUM` differ from `VACUUM FULL`?
choices: VACUUM only refreshes planner statistics; FULL is the one that actually removes dead tuples
VACUUM makes space reusable while traffic continues; FULL rewrites under an exclusive lock
VACUUM runs on indexes only; FULL also processes the table heap
VACUUM needs the table offline; FULL can run while traffic continues
questions.why: Plain VACUUM runs alongside reads and writes and makes dead space reusable, but rarely shrinks the file. VACUUM FULL rewrites the table compactly and returns space to the OS, holding an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that blocks everything. Tools such as pg_repack do the rewrite online.
questions.asked: Running VACUUM FULL on a live table causes outages; knowing the lock difference is the point.

questions.q: In Postgres, what does `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` change compared with a plain `CREATE INDEX` on a busy table?
choices: It builds faster, using several worker processes on the table
It builds the whole index in memory first, then swaps it into place atomically at the end
It lets writes continue during the build, but cannot run inside a transaction
It skips validation, so the index may be used before it is complete
questions.why: A plain CREATE INDEX blocks inserts, updates and deletes for the whole build. CONCURRENTLY takes a weaker lock and scans twice, so it is slower but writes continue. It cannot run in a transaction block, and if it fails it leaves an INVALID index you must drop and retry.
questions.asked: Adding an index to a hot table is a real production task; the INVALID-index caveat marks real experience.

questions.q: Why would you choose a B-tree index over a hash index in Postgres for a `created_at` column?
choices: Hash indexes are not crash-safe in any Postgres version
B-trees are smaller, since hash indexes store every value twice
Hash indexes cannot store timestamp values, only integers
B-trees support range queries and ORDER BY; hash only equality
questions.why: A hash index maps values to buckets with no ordering, so it answers `=` only. Timestamps are usually filtered by range and sorted, which needs a B-tree. Hash indexes have been WAL-logged and crash-safe since Postgres 10, and are rarely worth it over a B-tree.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know index types exist for reasons, not just 'CREATE INDEX' by default.

questions.q: An append-only `events` table in Postgres has 2 billion rows, inserted in time order and queried by time range. Which index type is tiny yet effective here?
choices: BRIN, which stores the min and max per block range
GIN, which indexes each timestamp as a separate key
Hash, which gives each timestamp its own bucket
GiST, which is designed for full-text documents
questions.why: Because rows arrive in time order, each block range covers a narrow time window, and BRIN records just the min and max per range, so it is kilobytes instead of gigabytes and lets Postgres skip ranges. It is useless if the physical order does not follow the column. GIN suits arrays, jsonb and full-text.
questions.asked: A good 'do you know beyond B-tree' question for logging and analytics tables.

questions.q: In Postgres, how can you make `WHERE name ILIKE '%smith%'` use an index?
choices: A B-tree index on lower(name), which also handles leading wildcards
A GIN index using gin_trgm_ops from the pg_trgm extension
A hash index on name, which matches any substring by hashing it
It cannot: a leading wildcard always means a full table scan
questions.why: pg_trgm splits text into three-character trigrams, and a GIN or GiST trigram index can find rows containing a substring, with or without case sensitivity. A B-tree only helps prefix patterns such as `'smith%'`. For word-based search with ranking, full-text search is the better tool.
questions.asked: Substring search is a frequent feature request; knowing pg_trgm shows you can solve it without a search engine.

questions.q: A list is sorted `ORDER BY priority DESC, created_at ASC` and is slow. In Postgres or SQL Server, which index lets it read rows already in order?
choices: (priority, created_at), as a B-tree can be read in either direction
(created_at, priority), as the most selective column goes first
(priority DESC, created_at ASC), matching the mixed directions
Two single-column indexes, which the planner merges into one order
questions.why: A B-tree can be scanned forwards or backwards, which serves (ASC, ASC) or (DESC, DESC), but not mixed directions. Declaring the index with the same mixed order, or its exact reverse, lets the sort be skipped. For single-column or same-direction sorts the direction does not matter.
questions.asked: Mixed-direction sorts are a subtle index-design case; getting it right shows you understand how B-trees are read.

questions.q: Writes to a table are slow and it has 14 indexes. In Postgres, how do you find indexes that are never used?
choices: Check pg_indexes for indexes whose definition has no WHERE clause
Run EXPLAIN on a single query and drop any index it does not mention
Drop them all, then re-add whichever ones users complain about when their pages get slow again
Check pg_stat_user_indexes for indexes whose idx_scan is 0 since the last reset
questions.why: Postgres counts scans per index in pg_stat_user_indexes; SQL Server has sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats. Check over a representative period (month-end jobs!), on every replica that serves reads, and keep indexes that enforce uniqueness even if they are never scanned.
questions.asked: Index hygiene is a practical ops question; the caveats about replicas and constraints show judgment.

questions.q: When is a Merge Join the natural choice for the planner?
choices: When both inputs are already sorted on the join key, for example by indexes
When the join condition uses inequality, such as a.x > b.y
When one input is tiny and the other has an index on the join key
When the two tables live on different servers, so their rows must be merged remotely
questions.why: A merge join walks two sorted inputs side by side, like merging two sorted lists, which is cheap when both arrive sorted and large. A small outer input with an indexed inner side favours a nested loop; large unsorted inputs favour a hash join. Merge and hash joins need an equality condition.
questions.asked: Knowing the three join algorithms and when each wins is standard plan-reading knowledge.

questions.q: Why can a Nested Loop join be the best plan, despite its name suggesting O(n x m) work?
choices: Because the planner parallelises each iteration of the loop across every available CPU core
Because with few outer rows, each inner lookup is a cheap index seek
Because it caches the inner table in memory after the first loop
Because it is used only when both tables have fewer than 1,000 rows
questions.why: With 10 outer rows and an index on the inner join key, a nested loop does 10 cheap seeks and returns the first rows immediately. It becomes a problem when the outer estimate is wrong and it actually loops 100,000 times, which is why misestimates show up as slow nested loops.
questions.asked: It checks you don't read operator names as good or bad, but reason from row counts.

questions.q: In SQL Server, what does a `Clustered Index Scan` on `Orders` in a plan usually mean?
choices: The query used the clustered index to jump straight to the matching rows
The clustered index is being rebuilt while the query is running
SQL Server read the whole table, since the clustered index is the table
Only the key columns were read, which is cheaper than any seek
questions.why: Because the clustered index holds the table's rows, scanning it is a full table scan. A Clustered Index Seek is the targeted form. Scans are fine for small tables or when most rows are needed; on a large table with a selective filter they point to a missing or unusable index.
questions.asked: Reading operator names correctly is the entry level of SQL Server plan reading.

questions.q: Which Postgres extension is the usual first step to find which queries use the most total time in production?
choices: pgcrypto, which hashes query texts so that they can be grouped together
pg_trgm, which records the text of every slow query in a trigram index
auto_explain on every single query, which writes each plan to the server log for later grepping
pg_stat_statements, which aggregates calls, time and rows per normalised query
questions.why: pg_stat_statements groups queries by shape and records calls, total and mean time, so you can sort by total time and fix what matters most, often a fast query called millions of times. auto_explain with a duration threshold complements it by logging plans of slow runs. SQL Server's equivalent is Query Store.
questions.asked: 'How would you find the slow queries?' is a standard question; naming the tool and sorting by total time is the strong answer.

questions.q: In SQLite, `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` for a query on `o (customer_id, created_at)` shows `SEARCH o USING COVERING INDEX ix (customer_id=?)`. What does that tell you?
choices: The index found the rows and held every needed column, so the table was skipped
The whole table was scanned, and the index was consulted per row
The query used the index for ORDER BY only, and filtered in a temp table
The index was created automatically just for this query, then discarded when it finished
questions.why: SEARCH means an index seek on the listed columns (SCAN means reading everything), and COVERING means all the selected columns were in the index, so no table lookup was needed. `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY` would mean an extra sort. Automatic indexes show as AUTOMATIC.
questions.asked: SQLite is common in tests and small apps; being able to read its plan output is a useful, quick skill.

questions.q: SQL Server's execution plan shows a green 'Missing Index' suggestion. How should you treat it?
choices: Create it as written, as the optimiser has proven it is the best index
Use it as a hint: check overlap with existing indexes and write costs first
Ignore it, as missing-index hints are shown only for estimated plans
Create it, but only after dropping the table's clustered index to make room for it on disk
questions.why: The suggestion is generated for one query in isolation; it ignores existing similar indexes, key-column order subtleties and the write cost. Consolidate it with what exists, often by widening an index with INCLUDE, rather than adding near-duplicates for every query.
questions.asked: Tables with 30 overlapping indexes usually come from accepting every hint; this checks your judgment.

questions.q: A job-queue table has 5 million done jobs and a few hundred pending ones. Workers run `WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY id`. In Postgres, which index is the best fit?
choices: A B-tree on status alone, as that is the column being filtered
A hash index on status, as the filter is an equality test
A partial index ON jobs (id) WHERE status = 'pending'
A BRIN index on id, as ids arrive in increasing order
questions.why: A partial index contains only the pending rows, so it stays tiny however many done jobs pile up, and it is ordered by id for the ORDER BY. The planner uses it when the query's WHERE implies the index's predicate. SQL Server calls these filtered indexes.
questions.asked: Queue and status tables are everywhere; the partial index is an elegant, practical answer.

questions.q: Why does `SELECT MAX(created_at) FROM orders` return instantly when `created_at` is indexed?
choices: The engine caches the maximum of every indexed column
The query is rewritten as ORDER BY with LIMIT 1 in memory
MAX is computed from table statistics, not the data
It reads one end of the sorted index instead of every row
questions.why: A B-tree is sorted, so the maximum is the last entry (ignoring NULLs): one short descent. It is also why `ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1` is fast. Statistics are only estimates and never used as query answers.
questions.asked: A small question that checks you think of indexes as sorted structures, not magic.

questions.q: What is the default transaction isolation level in both Postgres 17 and SQL Server 2022?
choices: READ COMMITTED, in both engines
READ UNCOMMITTED, for maximum throughput
REPEATABLE READ, in both engines
SERIALIZABLE, in both engines
questions.why: Both default to READ COMMITTED: each statement sees only committed data, but two reads in one transaction can see different values. SERIALIZABLE is available but opt-in because it costs retries or blocking; READ UNCOMMITTED is not the default anywhere mainstream.
questions.asked: Knowing the default tells you which anomalies your code is already exposed to without anyone choosing them.

questions.q: In Postgres, SQL Server (with `UPDLOCK`) or MySQL, what does `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` do inside a transaction?
choices: It copies the row into a private snapshot that nobody else can see
It locks the row so other writers wait until this transaction ends
It marks the row as dirty so other readers skip it until commit
It upgrades the whole transaction to SERIALIZABLE for its lifetime
questions.why: FOR UPDATE takes a row lock at read time, so a concurrent `FOR UPDATE` or UPDATE on row 7 blocks until COMMIT, closing the read-compute-write race. Plain readers in Postgres are not blocked (MVCC), and the isolation level is unchanged.
questions.asked: It is the simplest pessimistic fix for read-then-write races, and a strong answer says who is and is not blocked.

questions.q: What is a deadlock in a relational database?
choices: A query that waits on a lock longer than the configured timeout
