A transaction that holds locks and never commits because the app crashed
Two transactions each holding a lock the other one needs to proceed
A table lock taken because too many row locks were held at once
questions.why: A deadlock is a cycle: A waits for B's lock while B waits for A's, so neither can ever proceed. A long wait or an abandoned open transaction is blocking, which resolves when the holder finishes; a deadlock never resolves by itself.
questions.asked: Candidates often confuse deadlocks with slow blocking; the distinction decides whether you tune timeouts or fix lock ordering.

questions.q: Postgres or SQL Server detects a deadlock between two of your transactions. What does your application see?
choices: Each statement hangs until its command timeout fires
Each transaction is rolled back and each caller gets an error
The engine silently retries the second transaction after the first
One is rolled back with an error; the other one continues
questions.why: The engine picks a victim, aborts it with a deadlock error (Postgres SQLSTATE 40P01, SQL Server error 1205) and lets the survivor finish. Nothing is retried for you: the app should catch that error and retry the whole transaction.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear that deadlocks are expected occasionally and that the fix includes a retry path in code.

questions.q: `tags` holds ('sql', 1). In Postgres or SQLite, what does the final SELECT return?
choices: ('sql', 1), because the conflicting row is skipped
An error, because name is the primary key and is duplicated
('sql', 9), because the new values overwrite the old ones
Two rows, since DO NOTHING turns off the uniqueness check
questions.why: DO NOTHING swallows the unique violation for that row and leaves the existing one untouched. Overwriting needs `DO UPDATE SET uses = excluded.uses`; the constraint itself is never disabled.
questions.asked: Idempotent inserts are everywhere in webhooks and imports, so knowing the two ON CONFLICT forms is expected.

questions.q: In Postgres or SQLite 3.35+, `accounts` row 1 has balance 100. What does this statement return?
choices: 100, the value as it was before the update
70, the value after the update was applied
1, the number of rows the update affected
Nothing, since RETURNING only works on INSERT
questions.why: RETURNING evaluates against the new row version, so you get 70 in the same round trip. For the old value in SQL Server, `OUTPUT deleted.balance` gives the before image; the affected-row count comes from the driver, not RETURNING.
questions.asked: RETURNING removes a read-after-write round trip and a race, which is why reviewers like to see it.

questions.q: In Postgres, `data` is a jsonb column holding `{"age": 30}`. What is the difference between `data -> 'age'` and `data ->> 'age'`?
choices: `->` reads one level; `->>` searches all levels
`->` returns text; `->>` returns jsonb
`->` returns jsonb; `->>` returns text
`->` yields NULL if missing; `->>` raises an error
questions.why: `->` keeps the result as jsonb (good for chaining into nested objects), while `->>` extracts it as text, so `(data->>'age')::int > 18` is the usual filter. Neither searches recursively, and both yield NULL for a missing key.
questions.asked: Comparing a jsonb value to a string or number is a daily bug source, so interviewers check you know which operator yields what.

questions.q: In SQL Server 2022, `Data` holds `{"name":"Ann","tags":["a","b"]}` as nvarchar. What do `JSON_VALUE(Data, '$.tags')` and `JSON_QUERY(Data, '$.tags')` return?
choices: Each returns the array text; JSON_VALUE trims its whitespace
Each returns NULL, as arrays need OPENJSON to be read at all
JSON_VALUE returns 'a'; JSON_QUERY returns the whole array text
JSON_VALUE returns NULL (not a scalar); JSON_QUERY returns the array
questions.why: JSON_VALUE extracts scalars only and returns NULL in lax mode for objects or arrays; JSON_QUERY extracts objects and arrays. To turn the array into rows you would then use OPENJSON.
questions.asked: Picking the wrong function gives silent NULLs, a classic SQL Server JSON bug.

questions.q: `SELECT json_extract('{"a":{"b":[10,20]}}', '$.a.b[1]')` runs in SQLite. What does it return?
choices: 20, because JSON path indexes start at 0
10, because JSON path indexes start at 1
The text '[10,20]', since arrays are not indexed
NULL, since nested paths need json_each
questions.why: SQL/JSON paths (SQLite, MySQL, SQL Server, Postgres jsonpath) index arrays from 0, so `$.a.b[1]` is the second element, 20. Nested paths work directly; json_each is for turning arrays into rows.
questions.asked: JSON paths are the common syntax across engines, and off-by-one index errors are easy to make.

questions.q: In Postgres, what is the practical difference between the `json` and `jsonb` types?
choices: json is binary and indexable; jsonb keeps the original text as typed
jsonb is parsed and indexable; json keeps the exact text as typed
jsonb is only for arrays; json is for objects with named keys
They are aliases; jsonb is the newer name kept for compatibility
questions.why: jsonb stores a decomposed binary form: duplicate keys and key order are dropped, but it supports GIN indexes and containment operators. json stores the input text verbatim and reparses it on every access. jsonb is the right default for application data.
questions.asked: Choosing json by accident loses indexing, so interviewers expect jsonb as the default with a reason.

questions.q: Your product search uses `WHERE description LIKE '%running shoes%'`. Why is full-text search usually better for a search box?
choices: LIKE is case-sensitive on every engine, while full-text never is
LIKE cannot match text longer than an indexed column's length
Full-text search matches word forms and ranks results by relevance
Full-text search runs without an index, so writes stay fast
questions.why: Full-text search tokenises and stems text, so 'run' finds 'running' and word order or gaps do not matter, and it can rank matches; with a GIN or full-text index it avoids scanning every row. LIKE's case sensitivity depends on collation, and FTS does need its own index.
questions.asked: Search features are common in CRUD apps; a good answer knows when to reach for built-in FTS before an external engine.

questions.q: In Postgres, why does this return true?
questions.code:
SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'She was running late')
    @@ to_tsquery('english', 'run');
choices: `@@` does a substring match, and 'run' occurs inside 'running'
The english config treats every verb form as a stop word
to_tsquery adds a trailing wildcard to every term automatically
The english config stems 'running' and 'run' to the same lexeme
questions.why: Both sides go through the english dictionary, which reduces 'running' and 'run' to the lexeme 'run', so the match is on normalised words, not substrings. Prefix matching needs an explicit `run:*`; stop words like 'she' and 'was' are dropped, not verbs.
questions.asked: Understanding stemming explains both why FTS finds more and why it sometimes surprises users.

questions.q: In Postgres, SQL Server or SQLite, what does `top` hold on each row?
questions.code:
SELECT name, dept,
  FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER (
    PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS top
FROM employees;
choices: The name of the highest-paid employee in that row's department
The first employee name in the table, the same on every row
The row's own name when it is the top earner, otherwise NULL
The alphabetically first name within that row's department
questions.why: FIRST_VALUE takes the first row of each partition's window in the given order, so every row in a department sees that department's top earner. Unlike LAST_VALUE, the default frame does not trip it up, because the frame always starts at the partition's first row.
questions.asked: Showing each row next to its group's best is a common reporting request that avoids a self-join.

questions.q: In Postgres or SQLite, what does `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')` do in a grouped query?
choices: It removes unpaid rows from the whole query before grouping
It counts only the paid rows within each group
It counts the groups that contain at least one paid row overall
It is a HAVING condition that drops groups with no paid rows
questions.why: FILTER restricts which rows feed that one aggregate, so `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(*) FILTER (...)` can sit side by side in the same group. It is the standard-SQL form of `SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`; it neither filters the query nor the groups.
questions.asked: Dashboards need several conditional counts per row, and FILTER is the tidiest way to express them where supported.

questions.q: `daily` holds (day 1, 40), (day 2, 55), (day 3, 50). What does `ch` contain, in day order?
questions.code:
SELECT day, n - LAG(n, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS ch
FROM daily;
choices: NULL, 15, -5
15, -5, NULL
questions.why: LAG's third argument is the default when there is no previous row, so day 1 computes 40 - 0 = 40 rather than NULL. Without that default the first row would be NULL; the NULL at the end belongs to LEAD.
questions.asked: The default argument avoids a COALESCE, and remembering where LAG yields NULL shows real use.

questions.q: Under default settings in Postgres, transaction A has run `UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = 5` but not committed. What happens to other sessions?
choices: Readers and writers of row 5 both wait until A commits or rolls back
Nothing waits; the last transaction to commit overwrites the other
Readers see 'paid' already; another UPDATE of row 5 fails immediately
Readers see the old row; another UPDATE of row 5 waits for A to finish
questions.why: Postgres MVCC means plain SELECTs read the last committed version without blocking, but a second writer on the same row must wait for A's row lock. Dirty reads never happen in Postgres, and the second writer queues rather than failing.
questions.asked: Knowing that writers block writers but not readers is the basis for reasoning about any contention problem.

questions.q: A handler opens a transaction, updates an order, then calls a payment API that sometimes takes 20 seconds before committing. What is the main database problem?
choices: Its row locks are held through the API call, blocking writers
The transaction switches to autocommit after its first statement
The engine rolls back any transaction left idle for over a second
The API call's result is written to disk before the order row is
questions.why: Locks are held until COMMIT or ROLLBACK, so slow external calls inside a transaction make every other writer of those rows queue behind them and hold a pooled connection. Do the external call outside the transaction (or record intent and finish in a second short transaction).
questions.asked: Short transactions are a design rule; interviewers look for candidates who keep network I/O out of them.

questions.q: In Postgres, what does `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT` do when another transaction already holds a lock on the row?
choices: It waits for the lock, then returns the row as it now stands
It fails at once with a lock-not-available error you can handle
It returns the row anyway, ignoring the other transaction's lock
It returns no rows, silently skipping the ones that are locked
questions.why: NOWAIT turns the wait into an immediate error (SQLSTATE 55P03), useful when a user should be told 'someone else is editing this' instead of hanging. Silently skipping locked rows is SKIP LOCKED, which suits job queues rather than single-record edits.
questions.asked: Choosing between waiting, NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED shows you match the lock behaviour to the use case.

questions.q: What is a database trigger, and what is the most common complaint about using one for business rules?
choices: A scheduled job run by the engine; it cannot see the changed rows
A constraint checked at commit time; it cannot enforce cross-row rules
Code the engine runs on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE; its effects are hidden
A stored query that runs on read; it slows every SELECT on the table
questions.why: A trigger fires automatically on data changes and can see old and new rows, so it is good for audit trails or keeping derived data in sync. The complaint is invisibility: developers reading app code do not see the extra writes, and bulk operations get slower. Scheduled jobs are a separate feature.
questions.asked: Interviewers want a balanced view: triggers are fine for auditing, risky as a home for core business logic.

questions.q: In Postgres, `EXPLAIN` is run without `ANALYZE`. What do the row counts in its output represent?
choices: The exact table sizes, read from the files on disk at plan time
The actual rows read, measured by running the query in a rollback
The rows cached in memory at the time the plan was generated
The planner's estimates; the query is planned but not executed
questions.why: Plain EXPLAIN only plans the statement and shows estimated rows and costs from statistics. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually executes it and adds actual rows and timings, which is how you spot misestimates. Neither reads cache contents unless you ask for BUFFERS with ANALYZE.
questions.asked: Comparing estimates to actuals is the core diagnostic move, so knowing which one you are looking at matters.

questions.q: A Postgres plan for `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1` on 3 million rows shows `Seq Scan on users ... Filter: (email = $1) Rows Removed by Filter: 2999999`. What does this most likely indicate?
choices: There is no usable index on email for this lookup
The table's statistics are stale and it needs an ANALYZE
The query is correct; seq scans are always the fastest
The email column holds too many NULLs to be indexed
questions.why: Reading every row to keep one is the signature of a missing (or unusable) index: add one on email, or check the query is not wrapping the column in a function. Seq scans are right for small tables or low-selectivity filters, not a single-row lookup on a large one.
questions.asked: Reading 'Rows Removed by Filter' is the first plan skill anyone should have.

questions.q: Why not simply add an index on every column of a busy table?
choices: Engines refuse more than one index per table at a time
Each index slows every insert and update and takes space
Extra indexes make SELECT queries return rows in random order
Indexes on non-key columns disable the primary key index
questions.why: Every index must be updated on each write that touches its columns, costs disk and memory, and adds work for vacuum or maintenance. Engines allow many indexes, and indexes never change query results; you add them for the queries you actually run.
questions.asked: Indexes are a trade-off, and interviewers want to hear the write cost, not 'more is faster'.

questions.q: A team stores each post's tag ids in a JSON array column instead of a `post_tags` table. What do they lose?
choices: The ability to store more than a few ids in one row
Transactions on writes that touch the tag array
Foreign keys on the ids and simple, indexable joins
The ability to read tags back in the order written
questions.why: Ids inside JSON cannot reference `tags(id)`, so deleted tags leave dangling ids, and queries like 'posts with tag 5' need JSON functions instead of an indexed join. JSON arrays preserve order and are written transactionally like any other column.
questions.asked: JSON columns are tempting shortcuts, and interviewers check you know what relational guarantees you give up.

questions.q: Which isolation level makes concurrent transactions behave as if they had run one after another?
choices: READ COMMITTED
REPEATABLE READ
SNAPSHOT
SERIALIZABLE
questions.why: SERIALIZABLE guarantees the result equals some serial order, preventing every anomaly including write skew. REPEATABLE READ and SNAPSHOT still allow write skew (two transactions each reading, then writing different rows based on what they read).
questions.asked: It anchors the isolation ladder; a strong answer adds that it costs retries or blocking.

questions.q: Your app renames `users.fullname` to `display_name` in one migration during a rolling deploy. What breaks?
choices: Old app instances still query fullname and fail until replaced
Nothing, because the engine keeps the old name as an alias
The rename rewrites the whole table and locks it for minutes
New app instances fail because the rename runs after they start
questions.why: During a rolling deploy old and new code run side by side, so a rename breaks whichever version expects the other name. The zero-downtime pattern is expand and contract: add the new column, write both, backfill, switch reads, then drop the old one. A rename itself is a quick metadata change in most engines.
questions.asked: Expand and contract is the core zero-downtime migration idea and comes up in almost every deployment discussion.

questions.q: In Postgres, why prefer `id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` over the older `id bigserial`?
choices: Identity columns never leave gaps after a rolled-back insert
It is SQL-standard and blocks accidental manual id inserts
serial columns are removed in Postgres 17 and will not parse
Identity columns are faster because they avoid any sequence
questions.why: Identity is the standard syntax, ties the sequence cleanly to the column (ownership, permissions, dump/restore) and, with ALWAYS, rejects explicit id values unless you say OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE. It still uses a sequence under the hood, so gaps still happen; serial still works.
questions.asked: It shows you keep up with modern Postgres defaults rather than copying old tutorials.

questions.q: Under SERIALIZABLE in Postgres, a transaction fails with SQLSTATE 40001 (could not serialize access). What should the application do?
choices: Lower the isolation level for that session and resubmit it
Retry only the failing statement inside the same transaction
Retry the whole transaction from the start, a few times at most
Treat it as a bug in the query, since it cannot happen by design
questions.why: Serialization failures are the price of SERIALIZABLE's guarantee: the engine aborts one transaction instead of allowing an anomaly, and the correct response is to rerun the entire transaction, because its reads are now stale. The aborted transaction cannot continue, so retrying one statement fails.
questions.asked: Using SERIALIZABLE without a retry loop is a common mistake, and interviewers probe for it.

questions.q: What is table partitioning (Postgres declarative partitioning, SQL Server partitioned tables) mainly used for in an application database?
choices: Spreading one table's rows across several servers for write scaling
Keeping a hot copy of the table in memory for faster reads
Giving each tenant a separate schema with its own permissions
Splitting a huge table by a key such as month for pruning and drops
questions.why: Partitioning splits one logical table into child tables by range, list or hash, so queries filtering on the key touch only relevant partitions and old data can be removed by dropping a partition instead of a huge DELETE. It stays on one server; spreading across servers is sharding.
questions.asked: Time-series tables such as events or audit logs are the usual trigger, and interviewers want the retention benefit named.

questions.q: In Postgres, what does `WHERE data @> '{"status": "active"}'` match on a jsonb column, and why is it preferred?
choices: Rows whose data contains that key and value; a GIN index can serve it
Rows whose data equals exactly that object; a B-tree index serves it
Rows where any nested value contains 'active' as a substring match
Rows whose data has a status key, whatever its value happens to be
questions.why: `@>` is containment: the left document must include the right one (extra keys are fine), and a GIN index on data (jsonb_ops or jsonb_path_ops) accelerates it. `data->>'status' = 'active'` needs a separate expression index. Key existence alone is the `?` operator.
questions.asked: It shows you can query JSON in a way the index actually supports.

questions.q: What is a Postgres advisory lock (`pg_advisory_lock(key)`) typically used for in an application?
choices: Locking a table so that reads wait during a bulk import
Ensuring only one instance runs a job or migration at once
Preventing two users from editing the same row via the ORM
Warning the planner that a table is about to change a lot
questions.why: Advisory locks lock an application-chosen number, not a table or row, so several app instances can agree that only one runs the nightly job or migration at a time. They do not stop anyone touching data; row edits are protected with row locks or optimistic concurrency.
questions.asked: Once apps run several replicas, 'run this only once' needs a coordination primitive, and the database often already has one.

questions.q: A Postgres session has sat 'idle in transaction' for three hours. Besides holding locks, what harm does it do?
choices: It forces every other query to run under SERIALIZABLE
It doubles the WAL written by each concurrent transaction
It stops VACUUM removing dead rows newer than its snapshot
It pins its tables in memory, evicting other data from cache
questions.why: VACUUM can only remove row versions that no open transaction might still see, so one ancient transaction makes dead tuples pile up across the database, causing bloat and slower queries. `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` is the usual guard. It does not change others' isolation.
questions.asked: Bloat from forgotten transactions is a real production incident type, and naming the timeout setting is a plus.

questions.q: In Postgres 11+, what does `ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN source text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'web'` cost on a 50-million-row table?
choices: A full table rewrite under an exclusive lock, taking minutes
A rewrite in the background while reads and writes carry on
Nothing at all, because NOT NULL is checked lazily on later reads
A quick metadata change, since the constant default is stored once
questions.why: Since Postgres 11 a non-volatile default is stored in the catalogue and returned for old rows without rewriting them, so the ALTER needs only a brief lock. A volatile default such as `random()` or `clock_timestamp()` still forces a rewrite.
questions.asked: Knowing which DDL is instant and which rewrites the table is what lets you plan migrations without downtime.

questions.q: In SQL Server 2022, what do you need before `WHERE CONTAINS(Description, 'waterproof')` works?
choices: A full-text catalogue and full-text index on the table
A plain nonclustered index on the Description column
The database compatibility level set below 150
A computed column that stores Description in lower case
questions.why: CONTAINS and FREETEXT only work against a full-text index, which lives in a full-text catalogue and requires a unique key index on the table. A normal B-tree index cannot serve word searches, and full-text matching is case-insensitive anyway.
questions.asked: It tests whether you know full-text search is a separate feature you must set up, not a query trick.

questions.q: In Postgres, what makes full-text search over `articles.body` fast on a large table?
choices: A B-tree index on body, which sorts the words inside the text
A GIN index on to_tsvector('english', body), or a stored column
A hash index on body, since the search is an equality match
Nothing; @@ scans each row but is always fast enough in practice
questions.why: A GIN index maps each lexeme to the rows containing it; it must be built on exactly the same expression (same config) the query uses, or on a generated tsvector column. B-tree and hash indexes work on whole values, not words inside them.
questions.asked: Getting FTS to use its index is where most first attempts fail, so interviewers check the expression-match rule.

questions.q: Why do experienced SQL Server developers avoid adding `WITH (NOLOCK)` to report queries to stop blocking?
choices: NOLOCK makes the query take a table lock, which blocks everyone
It is ignored on tables that have a clustered index anyway
It reads uncommitted data and can skip or double-count rows
It forces a recompile of the plan on every single execution
questions.why: NOLOCK is READ UNCOMMITTED: it can return rows that later roll back and, during page splits, miss or duplicate rows. The safer fix for readers blocking writers is READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT (row versioning), which gives consistent committed reads without shared locks.
questions.asked: NOLOCK sprinkled everywhere is a code-review red flag, and knowing RCSI as the alternative is the strong answer.

questions.q: In SQL Server, what does the OUTPUT clause return in this statement?
choices: An error, since OUTPUT is only valid on INSERT and DELETE
The deleted and inserted row counts for the statement
The balance after the update, twice, for comparison
The balance before and after the update
questions.why: Inside OUTPUT, `deleted` is the before image and `inserted` the after image, so an UPDATE can return both, which Postgres RETURNING cannot do directly. OUTPUT works on INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE.
questions.asked: It is SQL Server's RETURNING, and audit or balance-change code uses it to avoid a second query.

questions.q: A Postgres migration runs `ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT ...` and the whole app freezes, though the ALTER itself is quick. Why, and what is the usual guard?
choices: The ALTER waits behind a long query and blocks all queued queries; set lock_timeout
The ALTER rewrites the table in place and blocks reads; add the constraint as NOT VALID
The ALTER triggers an autovacuum that blocks writes; run VACUUM FULL beforehand
The ALTER invalidates every cached plan at once; run DISCARD ALL on the pool
questions.why: ALTER needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock; while it waits behind a long-running SELECT, every later query queues behind the ALTER, so a quick DDL causes a full outage. `SET lock_timeout = '5s'` makes the migration fail fast and retry instead. NOT VALID helps with validation cost, not lock queueing.
questions.asked: Lock queueing behind DDL is the classic surprise outage in 'safe' migrations, and seniors know the lock_timeout habit.

questions.q: In SQL Server, a batch UPDATE touching 20,000 rows suddenly blocks unrelated queries on the same table. What is the likely mechanism?
choices: Page splits during the update force a full index rebuild
Lock escalation converted many row locks into a table lock
The update switched the database to SINGLE_USER mode
The optimiser chose a parallel plan that locks each partition
questions.why: SQL Server escalates to a table (or partition) lock once a statement holds roughly 5,000 locks on one object, trading memory for concurrency. Batching the update in smaller chunks keeps it below the threshold. Page splits and parallel plans do not lock the whole table.
questions.asked: Chunking large updates is standard practice, and escalation is the reason behind it.

questions.q: In SQLite, `orders.data` holds JSON like `{"items":["a","b"]}`. What does this query return for an order whose items array is empty?
questions.code:
SELECT o.id, j.value
FROM orders o, json_each(o.data, '$.items') j;
choices: One row with a NULL value, as a LEFT JOIN would
One row whose value is '[]', the raw array
No rows at all for that particular order
An error, as json_each needs a non-empty array
questions.why: json_each (like Postgres `jsonb_array_elements` or SQL Server `CROSS APPLY OPENJSON`) is a table-valued function producing one row per element, and the comma join is an inner join, so an empty array yields no rows. Keeping the order needs `LEFT JOIN json_each(...) ON true` or OUTER APPLY.
questions.asked: Turning a JSON array into rows is how you report on semi-structured data, and dropped parents are the usual bug.
